reasoning: Read numbduck/pybridge.py in full (current tree). Line 52 is the only gate: `if not isinstance(conn, duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection): raise TypeError(...)`. No other check (type identity, version/coordination guard, sentinel, etc.) precedes the raw walk anywhere in the function or in any caller (grepped all call sites: examples/fraud_score.py:153, examples/irr.py:231, examples/haversine.py:124, examples/online_scoring.py:152, test/test_ducklib.py:2569/2626/2724 -- none add extra validation before calling extract_connection_ptr). Lines 58-59 (`py_obj_addr = id(conn); cpp_obj_p = ctypes.c_void_p.from_address(py_obj_addr + 16).value`), 61-62 (`conn_ptr = ctypes.c_void_p.from_address(cpp_obj_p + 32).value`), and 67 (`ducklib.duckdb_query(conn_ptr, ...)`) match the finding's line citations exactly. isinstance() is a nominal-type check, not a layout proof, and this is not exploit folklore -- it is standard, well-documented Python semantics: (1) a metaclass overriding `__instancecheck__` on the class object referenced by `duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection` (achievable by monkeypatching the module attribute in-process) makes isinstance() return True for an arbitrary object with no C++ backing at all; (2) a Python subclass of DuckDBPyConnection also satisfies isinstance trivially. Either bypass drives id(conn)+16 and cpp_obj_p+32 to read whatever bytes happen to sit at those relative offsets in the attacker-supplied object, which are then fed to duckdb_query as a connection pointer -- a real, attacker-influenced pointer walk, not a hypothetical. The project's own understanding note (docs/reviews/2026-07-01-numbduck/understanding/bridge.md section 3.1 and section 5) independently reaches the identical conclusion ('This guards the Python type only; it does not guarantee the pybind11/ABI layout matches the offsets below') before this finding was authored, corroborating rather than being copied verbatim into the finding. The 'low' severity is well-calibrated, not overstated: exploiting this requires the caller to already be executing arbitrary Python in the same process (to monkeypatch the class or metaclass), at which point that caller already has unrestricted memory access via ctypes directly, so the finding correctly frames this as a hardening/documentation gap rather than a boundary-crossing vulnerability -- exactly the caveat baked into the finding's own severity justification. No contract-satisfied-elsewhere, no version/platform mitigation, and no evidence the finding mischaracterizes the code was found.
